in2-si-basic.shortcut: 24% is 25% less 1%: a quarter of 12,000 is 3,000, minus 120 gives ₹2,880. Or 8% of 12,000 is 960 a year, × 3.
in2-si-basic.trap: ₹3,120 — rounding 24% up to 25% (₹3,000) and then adding the 1% (₹120) instead of taking it off.

in2-si-find-principal.shortcut: 35% of P is 1,750, so 1% of P is 50 and P is 5,000. Back-check: 7% of 5,000 is 350 a year, × 5 = 1,750.
in2-si-find-principal.trap: ₹4,500 looks right if 1,750 ÷ 0.35 is estimated rather than worked; 35% of 4,500 is only ₹1,575, short of the ₹1,750 stated.

in2-si-find-rate.shortcut: 1% of 8,000 is 80, so ₹1,920 is 24% of the principal; spread over 4 years that is 6% a year.
in2-si-find-rate.trap: 5% — dividing by the amount (₹9,920) instead of the principal gives about 4.8%, which rounds to it. Simple interest is always a percentage of the principal.

in2-si-find-time.shortcut: ₹1,800 is 30% of 6,000, and at 5% a year it takes 30 ÷ 5 = 6 years to build 30%.
in2-si-find-time.trap: 5 — taking 5% of the amount ₹7,800 (₹390 a year) gives about 4.6 years, which rounds to it; interest is charged on the ₹6,000 only.

in2-si-doubles-in-eight.shortcut: Doubling means the interest equals P, so each of the 8 years must earn 1/8 of P — and 1/8 = 12.5%.
in2-si-doubles-in-eight.trap: 12% — truncating 100 ÷ 8 to a whole number; 12% for 8 years is only 96%, just short of doubling.

in2-si-triples.shortcut: At 10% the interest adds one more P every 10 years: 2P at year 10, 3P at year 20.
in2-si-triples.trap: 10 — that is when the sum doubles (100% interest); tripling needs 200% interest, twice as long.

in2-si-doubles-then-quadruples.shortcut: Doubling in 10 years fixes the rate at 10% a year; four times needs 300% interest, and 300 ÷ 10 = 30 years.
in2-si-doubles-then-quadruples.trap: 20 — doubling the doubling time as if the interest compounded (2 → 4 in another 10 years). Under simple interest 20 years only triples the sum.

in2-ci-two-years.shortcut: Step it: year one earns ₹2,000, year two earns 10% of 22,000 = ₹2,200, total ₹4,200.
in2-ci-two-years.trap: ₹4,000 — taking 10% for 2 years as a flat 20%, which is simple interest; the second year also earns 10% on the first year's ₹2,000.

in2-ci-three-years.shortcut: Add 10% three times: 10,000 → 11,000 → 12,100 → 13,310. Each step adds a copy of the last figure shifted one place.
in2-ci-three-years.trap: ₹13,000 — adding a flat 30%, which is the simple-interest amount; compounding adds interest on interest, ₹310 more.

in2-ci-minus-si-two-years.shortcut: The gap is only year two's interest on year one's interest: year one earns ₹800, and 10% of 800 is ₹80.
in2-ci-minus-si-two-years.trap: ₹100 is the tempting round figure, but it would need interest-on-interest at 12.5%; at 10% the ₹800 first-year interest earns just ₹80.

in2-ci-minus-si-find-principal.shortcut: At 5% the two-year gap is always P ÷ 400, since (1/20)² = 1/400, so P = 50 × 400. Check: ₹1,000 of first-year interest earns 5% = ₹50.
in2-ci-minus-si-find-principal.trap: ₹25,000 — writing 0.05² as 0.002 instead of 0.0025; 50 ÷ 0.002 gives exactly it.

in2-ci-half-yearly.shortcut: Two 10% periods compound to 21% (10 + 10 + 1), and 21% of 8,000 is ₹1,680.
in2-ci-half-yearly.trap: ₹1,600 — applying 20% once, as if compounding were annual; the second half-year also earns 10% on the first half's ₹800.

in2-ci-quarterly.shortcut: Quarterly compounding beats a flat 8% (₹10,800) by only a few tens of rupees, so ₹10,824 is the only option that fits; ₹10,850 would need 8.5%.
in2-ci-quarterly.trap: ₹10,800 — applying a flat 8% for the year, which ignores the interest each quarter earns on the quarters before.

in2-ci-principal-from-amount.shortcut: 9,261 is 21³ and 1.05 is 21/20, so the principal is 20³ = ₹8,000.
in2-ci-principal-from-amount.trap: ₹8,400 — dividing by 1.05 only twice (9,261 ÷ 1.1025); three years means three divisions, and ₹8,400 is the amount after the first year.

in2-ci-successive-amounts.shortcut: 4,410 = 4,000 × 1.05², a recognisable 5% amount; 5% of 4,410 is 220.50, which confirms it at once.
in2-ci-successive-amounts.trap: 6% — treating it as simple interest: ₹220.50 a year puts the principal at 4,410 − 441 = ₹3,969, and 220.50 ÷ 3,969 ≈ 5.6%.

in2-si-successive-amounts.trap: ₹1,440 — subtracting the ₹120 difference once from ₹1,560; that ₹120 covers two years, so three years of interest is ₹180.

in2-si-two-parts.shortcut: At 8% on all ₹2,600 the interest would be ₹208; the extra ₹22 comes from the 2% gap on the 10% part, so that part is 22 ÷ 0.02 = ₹1,100.
in2-si-two-parts.trap: ₹1,000 — it gives ₹100 + ₹128 = ₹228, close enough to ₹230 that a rough check passes it; the missing ₹2 needs another ₹100 at the 2% gap.

in2-si-rate-difference.shortcut: 3% extra for 4 years is 12% of the sum, so 1% of the sum is 300 ÷ 12 = 25 and the sum is ₹2,500.
in2-si-rate-difference.trap: ₹3,000 — it looks right because ₹300 is a neat 10% of it, but the extra rate over 4 years is 12%, which on ₹3,000 gives ₹360.

in2-ci-doubles-in-five.shortcut: Chain the doublings — 1 → 2 by year 5, 2 → 4 by year 10, 4 → 8 by year 15 — instead of scaling the multiple.
in2-ci-doubles-in-five.trap: 20 — counting 8 ÷ 2 = 4 doublings; 8 is 2³, so three doublings of 5 years each.

in2-ci-triples-in-four.shortcut: 1 → 3 takes 4 years and 3 → 9 takes the same 4 years, because each 4-year stretch multiplies by 3: 8 years.
in2-ci-triples-in-four.trap: 12 — counting 9 ÷ 3 = 3 triplings instead of 9 = 3²; two triplings reach nine times.

in2-si-total-interest-two-rates.shortcut: Per year: 6% of 5,000 = 300 and 8% of 4,000 = 320, so ₹620 a year and ₹1,240 over two.
in2-si-total-interest-two-rates.trap: ₹1,280 — swapping the rates (8% on ₹5,000 and 6% on ₹4,000), which gives ₹800 + ₹480.

in2-si-amount-after-time.shortcut: One multiplication: 15,000 × 1.36. A third of 15,000 is 5,000 and 36% is 400 more, so the interest is ₹5,400 and the amount ₹20,400.
in2-si-amount-after-time.trap: ₹21,000 — rounding the rate up to 10% (40% of 15,000 = 6,000); at 9% the four years add 36%, only ₹5,400.

in2-ci-population-style.shortcut: 4% is a factor of 26/25 and 6,250 = 625 × 10, so the amount is 10 × 26² = ₹6,760 with no decimals.
in2-ci-population-style.trap: ₹6,500 — stopping after the first year's growth (6,250 + 250); the second year adds 4% of 6,500 = ₹260.

in2-si-fraction-of-principal.shortcut: The interest is 1/8 of P over 3 years, so 1/24 of P a year, and 100 ÷ 24 = 4⅙%.
in2-si-fraction-of-principal.trap: 4% — rounding 12.5% ÷ 3 down to a whole number; 4% for 3 years is only 12%, short of the 12.5% needed.

in2-si-equal-amounts.shortcut: ₹400 is 40% of 1,000, and 40% at 5% a year takes 40 ÷ 5 = 8 years.
in2-si-equal-amounts.trap: 7 — compounding the 5% (1.05⁷ ≈ 1.407 reaches ₹1,400 in about 7 years); simple interest adds a flat ₹50 a year.

in2-ci-first-year-interest.shortcut: Multiply by 1.1 without finding P: 500 × 1.1 = ₹550, and the same step gives ₹605 for year three.
in2-ci-first-year-interest.trap: ₹500 — assuming each year's interest is the same, which holds only under simple interest; compound interest also charges 10% on the first ₹500.

in2-si-borrow-and-lend.shortcut: One step: the 2% gap for 3 years is 6% of 5,000 = ₹300.
in2-si-borrow-and-lend.trap: ₹600 — that is the interest he pays on the loan (4% × 3 years of ₹5,000), not his gain; the gain is only the 2% margin.

in2-si-sum-of-two-interests.trap: ₹2,800 echoes the ₹280 and looks right if the gap is taken as 10% of the sum; the actual gap is 24% − 10% = 14%, which on ₹2,800 would be ₹392.

in2-ci-effective-rate-two-years.shortcut: Grow a base of 100 twice: 100 → 120 → 144, so the overall rise is 44%.
in2-ci-effective-rate-two-years.trap: 40% — adding 20% + 20% as if it were simple interest; the second year's 20% also applies to the first year's 20, adding 4 more.

in2-si-installments.shortcut: Carry everything to the end of year 2: ₹1,000 grows to ₹1,100, while the first instalment earns a year's 5%, so 2.05x = 1,100 and x ≈ ₹537.
in2-si-installments.trap: ₹550 — splitting the ₹1,100 owed after two years into equal halves, forgetting that the first payment, made a year early, clears part of the debt and earns its own 5%.

in2-ci-amount-after-half-year-partial.shortcut: 5% for three periods on 8,000 is 8,000 × (21/20)³, and since 8,000 = 20³ that is 21³ = ₹9,261.
in2-ci-amount-after-half-year-partial.trap: ₹9,300 is the tempting round figure just above the simple-interest ₹9,200; half-yearly compounding adds only ₹61 over simple interest here, landing on ₹9,261.

in2-si-average-rate.shortcut: Add the rate-years: 5 × 2 + 8 × 3 + 10 × 2 = 54, so the interest is 54% of ₹10,000.
in2-si-average-rate.trap: ₹5,600 — swapping the stretches, giving 8% two years and 10% three (10 + 16 + 30 = 56%); 'thereafter' covers only years 6 and 7.

in2-ci-difference-three-years.shortcut: At 10%, every ₹1,000 has a three-year gap of ₹31 (1,331 − 1,300), so ₹93 = 3 × 31 means ₹3,000.
in2-ci-difference-three-years.trap: ₹3,500 or ₹4,000 tempt a solver who guesses from the size of the gap; at ₹31 per ₹1,000 they would give ₹108.50 and ₹124, not ₹93.

in2-si-simple-vs-compound-same.shortcut: Try ₹100 at 10%: both schemes pay ₹10 in year one; in year two compound pays ₹11 against ₹10. The tie holds only for the first period.
in2-si-simple-vs-compound-same.trap: "They are never equal" — assuming compounding always earns more; it only pulls ahead once there is interest to earn interest, after the first year.

di2-revenue-highest-growth.shortcut: Compare multiples, not differences: Gamma triples (80 → 240) while every other company less than doubles, so no percentages are needed.
di2-revenue-highest-growth.trap: "Beta" — its rise of ₹100 crore is the largest in rupees, but on a base of 200 it is only 50%.

di2-revenue-total-2024.shortcut: Pair the column: 180 + 180 = 360 and 240 + 160 = 400, so the total is 760.
di2-revenue-total-2024.trap: ₹740 crore — taking Delta's 160 (its 2022 figure, a number that also sits in the 2024 column as Gamma's) instead of its 180.

di2-revenue-share-of-beta.shortcut: Pair 210 + 250 = 460 and 300 + 240 = 540: the 2025 total is exactly 1,000, so Beta's 300 is 30% on sight.
di2-revenue-share-of-beta.trap: 40% — dividing Beta's 300 by the other three companies' 700 instead of the full 1,000 gives about 43%, which rounds to it.

di2-revenue-average-alpha.shortcut: Alpha rises by a steady 30 a year, so its average is the midpoint of the two middle years: (150 + 180) ÷ 2 = 165.
di2-revenue-average-alpha.trap: ₹150 crore — grabbing a 'middle' value from the row (Alpha's 2023 figure); with four evenly spaced values the mean lies halfway between the second and third.

di2-revenue-ratio.shortcut: Back-check the option: 3 : 5 means Gamma is 60% of Delta, and 60% of 200 is 120.
di2-revenue-ratio.trap: 2 : 3 — pairing Gamma's 120 with Delta's 2024 figure (180) instead of its 2023 figure (200).

di2-revenue-decline.shortcut: Only the Beta and Delta rows are not steadily rising; each has one dip, and the dips fall in different years (Beta 2023, Delta 2024).
di2-revenue-decline.trap: "Only in 2023" — stopping at Beta's dip (200 → 180) and missing Delta's fall from 200 to 180 a year later.

di2-students-percentage-girls.shortcut: 220/300 = 11/15; 1/15 is 6⅔%, so 11/15 is 73⅓%. Or: 225 girls would be 75%, and 220 is a little under.
di2-students-percentage-girls.trap: 75% — reading 220 out of 300 as roughly three-quarters; exactly three-quarters would need 225 girls.

di2-students-ratio-boys-girls.shortcut: Boys outnumber girls in Science, so the first term must be the larger — that rules out 2 : 3 and 3 : 4; 240 : 160 ÷ 80 = 3 : 2.
di2-students-ratio-boys-girls.trap: 2 : 3 — writing girls first; the question asks for boys to girls.

di2-students-share-of-total.shortcut: With a total of exactly 1,000, a share in percent is the count ÷ 10: 400 → 40%.
di2-students-share-of-total.trap: 30% — the share of Commerce or Arts (300 students each), picked up by reading the wrong row's total.

di2-students-more-boys.shortcut: Compare boys with half of each stream's total: 240 > 200 and 180 > 150 lead, while 80 < 150 does not.
di2-students-more-boys.trap: "None" — reading the totals row, where boys and girls are level at 500; equal totals hide two boy-heavy streams balanced by one girl-heavy stream.

di2-students-difference.shortcut: The gap equals |2 × boys − total|: Science 80, Commerce 60, Arts 140. Arts is also the only stream where one side is under a third.
di2-students-difference.trap: "Science" — taking boys minus girls with its sign, so Arts' 80 − 220 = −140 looks the smallest; the size of the gap is what counts.

di2-expense-amount.shortcut: 35% of 80 equals 80% of 35 = 28, which is quicker to do in the head.
di2-expense-amount.trap: ₹24 lakh — taking only the 30% part (0.3 × 80) and dropping the extra 5% (₹4 lakh).

di2-expense-difference.shortcut: 1% of ₹60 lakh is ₹0.6 lakh and the two heads are 10 points apart, so ₹6 lakh. Check: 15 − 9 = 6.
di2-expense-difference.trap: ₹10 lakh — reading the 10-point gap as ₹10 lakh without applying it to the ₹60 lakh total.

di2-expense-ratio.shortcut: Rent is the larger head, so the first term must be bigger — that leaves 4 : 3, 3 : 2 and 2 : 1; 20 : 15 divides by 5 to 4 : 3.
di2-expense-ratio.trap: 3 : 4 — reversing the order, marketing first; the question asks for rent to marketing.

di2-expense-total-from-part.shortcut: 20% is one-fifth, so the total is 15 × 5 = ₹75 lakh.
di2-expense-total-from-part.trap: ₹60 lakh — dividing by 25% (the raw-materials row) instead of rent's 20%; 15 ÷ 0.25 = 60.

di2-expense-angle.shortcut: 25% is a quarter of the circle, and a quarter of 360° is a right angle: 90°.
di2-expense-angle.trap: 72° — 360° ÷ 5, as if all five heads had equal slices; that is rent's 20%, not raw materials' 25%.

di2-production-total-unit.shortcut: Unit B rises by 50 a month, so its total is (first + last) × 4 ÷ 2 = (300 + 450) × 2 = 1,500.
di2-production-total-unit.trap: 1,600 — multiplying March's 400 by four as if it were the average; the average of 300 to 450 is 375.

di2-production-highest-month.shortcut: Compare March and April directly: April gains 50 in A and 50 in B but loses 150 in C, so March is ahead by 50; January and February are far lower.
di2-production-highest-month.trap: "April" — it leads in two of the three columns, but Unit C's drop from 600 to 450 leaves its total at 1,450 against March's 1,500.

di2-production-average-per-month.shortcut: Work from 500: the deviations 0, −100, +100, −50 sum to −50, and −50 ÷ 4 = −12.5, giving 487.5.
di2-production-average-per-month.trap: 500 — seeing +100 and −100 cancel and taking 500 as the average, forgetting that April's 450 pulls it down by 12.5.

di2-production-percentage-increase.shortcut: 150 on a base of 400 is 3/8, and 3/8 = 37.5%.
di2-production-percentage-increase.trap: 27.5% — dividing the rise of 150 by April's 550 instead of January's 400 gives 27.3%, which rounds to it.

di2-production-which-unit-fell.shortcut: Units A and B climb by exactly 50 every month, so only C, the irregular column, can fall — and 600 → 450 does.
di2-production-which-unit-fell.trap: "None of them" — assuming the steady monthly rises of Units A and B hold for every column; C falls from 600 to 450.

di2-caselet-college-admissions.shortcut: Chain the fractions: 40% × ¼ = 10%, and 10% of 1,200 = 120.
di2-caselet-college-admissions.trap: 100 — splitting the 1,200 equally among the three colleges (400 each) before taking a quarter; College A took 40%, which is 480.

di2-caselet-college-c.shortcut: C's share is 100 − 75 = 25%, a quarter of 1,200 = 300.
di2-caselet-college-c.trap: 420 — that is College B's 35% of 1,200; reading the wrong college's share.

di2-caselet-factory-shifts.shortcut: Shift sizes are 3 : 2, so the average sits 3/5 of the way from 12 to 15: 12 + 1.8 = 13.8.
di2-caselet-factory-shifts.trap: 13.2 — weighting the wrong way (2/5 of the way from 12 to 15), as if the smaller night shift were the larger.

di2-caselet-shop-profit.shortcut: Take 20% on the whole ₹22,000 (₹4,400), then add the extra 5% on Y's ₹12,000 (₹600): ₹5,000.
di2-caselet-shop-profit.trap: ₹4,400 — applying X's 20% to the combined revenue of ₹22,000, missing the higher 25% margin on Y.

di2-caselet-survey.shortcut: 280 + 220 is exactly 500, so the 90 counted twice must equal the number counted zero times: neither = both = 90.
di2-caselet-survey.trap: 100 is the tempting round figure, but it needs exactly 400 readers of at least one paper; 280 + 220 − 90 = 410, leaving 90.

di2-caselet-survey-only-a.shortcut: Only A = readers of at least one paper minus all of B's readers: 410 − 220 = 190.
di2-caselet-survey-only-a.trap: 220 — B's total, the figure printed beside A's in the prompt; 'only A' is A's 280 less the 90 who read both.

di2-caselet-budget-split.shortcut: Work in parts: build's 5 plus half of testing's 4 is 7 of 12 parts, and 7 × 40,000 = ₹2,80,000.
di2-caselet-budget-split.trap: ₹2,00,000 — the build budget before the transfer; half of testing (₹80,000) still has to be added.

di2-caselet-attendance.shortcut: Guess 84 and check the deviations: −4, +8, −8, +4, 0 sum to zero, so 84 is the average.
di2-caselet-attendance.trap: 82 — averaging the first and last days (80 and 84), a shortcut that works only when the figures rise evenly.

di2-caselet-target-shortfall.shortcut: She needs 240 more to reach 600, plus the extra 10% of 600 (60): 300.
di2-caselet-target-shortfall.trap: 240 — meeting the target exactly (600 − 360) and forgetting the extra 10% of 600.

di2-caselet-two-departments.shortcut: Weights 40 : 60 put the average 60% of the way from ₹30,000 to ₹50,000: 30,000 + 12,000 = ₹42,000.
di2-caselet-two-departments.trap: ₹40,000 — the plain midpoint of the two averages, which ignores that engineering has more people.

di2-caselet-discount-scheme.shortcut: Take the discount off the bill in one step: 20% of 1,500 is 300, and 2,400 − 300 = ₹2,100.
di2-caselet-discount-scheme.trap: ₹1,920 — discounting the whole ₹2,400 by 20%; only the ₹1,500 food portion gets the discount.

di2-caselet-fuel-cost.shortcut: Fuel costs ₹10 a kilometre (₹100 ÷ 10 km); the fleet drives 12 × 150 = 1,800 km, so ₹18,000.
di2-caselet-fuel-cost.trap: ₹15,000 — it echoes the 15 litres a van, but it is the cost of 10 vans, not 12; 15 litres × ₹100 × 12 = ₹18,000.

ma2-two-rice-varieties.shortcut: ₹35 is a third of the way from ₹30 to ₹45, so the dearer rice is one part in three: 2 : 1.
ma2-two-rice-varieties.trap: 1 : 2 — writing the distances 5 : 10 in the same order as the prices instead of crossing them; that mix would average ₹40.

ma2-tea-blend-profit.shortcut: ₹64.50 is a quarter of the way from ₹62 to ₹72 (2.5 of 10), so the dearer tea is one part in four: 3 : 1.
ma2-tea-blend-profit.trap: 1 : 3 — keeping the distances 2.5 : 7.5 uncrossed; that blend would cost ₹69.50 a kg.

ma2-milk-water-cost.shortcut: Selling at milk's own cost price, the whole gain comes from free water, so the water must be 25% of the milk bought: 1 : 4.
ma2-milk-water-cost.trap: 1 : 3 — making water 25% of the mixture rather than 25% of the milk; 1 : 3 gives a 33⅓% gain.

ma2-replace-milk-twice.shortcut: Each draw takes 10% of whatever milk is there: 40 → 36 → 32.4.
ma2-replace-milk-twice.trap: 36 L — stopping after one replacement; the second draw removes a further 3.6 L of milk.

ma2-replace-three-times.trap: 64.8 L — stopping one draw short (80 × 0.9² instead of 80 × 0.9³).

ma2-alloy-copper-tin.shortcut: 45% is nearer 60%, so A must be the larger share — only 5 : 3 and 4 : 3 qualify, and 4 : 3 gives (240 + 60) ÷ 7 ≈ 42.9%, so 5 : 3.
ma2-alloy-copper-tin.trap: 3 : 5 — pairing each alloy with its own distance from 45 (15 for A, 25 for B) instead of crossing them; that mix is only 35% copper.

ma2-average-price-of-mixture.shortcut: Quantities 15 : 25 = 3 : 5, so the price is 3/8 of the way from ₹32 to ₹40: 32 + 3 = ₹35.
ma2-average-price-of-mixture.trap: ₹36 — the plain mean of ₹40 and ₹32, which ignores that there is more of the cheaper sugar.

ma2-milk-water-ratio-after-adding.shortcut: Milk stays 36 L and water becomes 19 L; 19 is prime and does not divide 36, so the ratio cannot reduce — only 36 : 19 fits.
ma2-milk-water-ratio-after-adding.trap: 2 : 1 — the neat ratio 36 : 19 nearly is; it would need 18 L of water, i.e. 9 L added rather than 10.

ma2-two-vessels-equal.shortcut: The milk fractions 5/8 and 5/12 average to (30 + 20)/96 = 25/48, so water is 23/48: 25 : 23.
ma2-two-vessels-equal.trap: 5 : 4 — scaling the first vessel to 24 L (15 : 9) but adding the second unscaled as 5 : 7, giving 20 : 16; equal capacity means equal volumes.

ma2-quantity-of-water-to-add.shortcut: Back-check the option: 18 + 10 = 28 L of water against 42 L of milk is 3 : 2.
ma2-quantity-of-water-to-add.trap: 6 L — raising water from 30% to 40% of the original 60 L (24 L); adding water grows the total, so 40% of 70 L is what is needed.

ma2-acid-concentration.shortcut: Alligate the 20% solution with 100% acid at 50%: (100 − 50) : (50 − 20) = 5 : 3, so 50 L of solution takes 30 L of acid.
ma2-acid-concentration.trap: 25 L — adding half the volume on the hunch that half makes 50%; it gives 35 L of acid in 75 L, only about 46.7%.

ma2-profit-from-mixture.shortcut: Read it off the ratio: 1 L of free water per 4 L of paid milk is a 1/4 = 25% gain; a 1 : 3 mix would give 33⅓%.
ma2-profit-from-mixture.trap: 20% — measuring the free litre against the 5 L of mixture instead of the 4 L he paid for.

me2-rectangle-area-from-ratio.shortcut: Sides 3k and 2k give 5k = 40, so k = 8 and the area is 6k² = 6 × 64 = 384.
me2-rectangle-area-from-ratio.trap: 400 cm² — splitting the half-perimeter 40 equally into a 20 × 20 square, ignoring the 3 : 2 ratio.

me2-square-diagonal-area.shortcut: The diagonal splits the square into two triangles, each ½ × 8 × 4 = 16, so the area is 32.
me2-square-diagonal-area.trap: 16 cm² — taking the side as half the diagonal (4 cm); the side is 8 ÷ √2 ≈ 5.66 cm.

me2-circle-area-from-radius.shortcut: Remember r = 7 → 154 cm²; doubling the radius to 14 quadruples the area: 4 × 154 = 616.
me2-circle-area-from-radius.trap: 308 cm² — cancelling 14 against the 7 in 22/7 but dropping the resulting 2, so 22 × 14 instead of 22 × 2 × 14.

me2-circumference-from-area.shortcut: Once r = 7, circumference = 2 × area ÷ r = 2 × 154 ÷ 7 = 44 cm.
me2-circumference-from-area.trap: 22 cm — computing πr (22/7 × 7) and forgetting the 2 in 2πr; that is only half the circle.

me2-triangle-heron.shortcut: Split the 14 cm side as 5 + 9: the 5-12-13 and 9-12-15 right triangles share a height of 12, so the area is ½ × 14 × 12 = 84.
me2-triangle-heron.trap: 91 cm² — treating 13 and 14 as the legs of a right triangle (½ × 13 × 14); the triangle is not right-angled.

me2-equilateral-triangle-area.shortcut: The height is half the side times √3, i.e. 6√3, so the area is ½ × 12 × 6√3 = 36√3.
me2-equilateral-triangle-area.trap: 72 cm² — using ½ × base × side, as if the 12 cm side were the height; the height is only 6√3 ≈ 10.4 cm.

me2-cuboid-volume.shortcut: Pair the 5 with the 12 first: 12 × 5 = 60, then 60 × 8 = 480. The volume must be a multiple of 96 (12 × 8), and only 480 is.
me2-cuboid-volume.trap: 440 cm³ — slipping 12 × 8 to 88 (as if 11 × 8) and multiplying by 5; 12 × 8 is 96.

me2-cuboid-surface-area.shortcut: Group it as top and bottom plus the band of walls: 2 × 60 + 2 × 4 × (10 + 6) = 120 + 128 = 248.
me2-cuboid-surface-area.trap: 188 cm² — leaving out one 10 × 6 face, as for an open box; a closed cuboid has all six faces.

me2-cube-diagonal.shortcut: Space diagonal² = 3a² = 108, so the diagonal is √108 = 6√3 ≈ 10.4 cm — longer than a face diagonal (≈ 8.5) but shorter than 12.
me2-cube-diagonal.trap: 6√2 cm — the diagonal of one face; the question asks for the diagonal through the cube.

me2-cylinder-curved-surface.shortcut: For r = 7, 2πr is 44; multiply by the height: 44 × 10 = 440.
me2-cylinder-curved-surface.trap: 748 cm² — adding the two circular ends (2πr(r + h) = 44 × 17), which is the total surface, not the curved one.

me2-sphere-volume.trap: 132 cm³ — slipping 792 ÷ 7 to 792 ÷ 6 when finishing 36 × 22/7; dividing by 7 gives 113.1.

me2-cone-volume.shortcut: A third of the height is 4, and πr² for r = 7 is 154, so the volume is 154 × 4 = 616.
me2-cone-volume.trap: 528 cm³ — multiplying the base circumference (44) by the height, a surface-style product rather than (1/3)πr²h.

me2-path-around-garden.shortcut: Path area = garden perimeter × width + four corner squares: 160 × 2 + 4 × 4 = 336.
me2-path-around-garden.trap: 316 m² — forgetting the four 2 × 2 corners gives 320, and 316 is the nearest option to it; the corners add 16, making 336.

me2-carpet-cost.shortcut: Multiply the easy pair first: 15 × 40 = 600, then 600 × 12 = ₹7,200.
me2-carpet-cost.trap: ₹8,000 looks right as a round figure (200 m² × ₹40), but the room is 15 × 12 = 180 m², not 200.

me2-parallelogram-area.trap: 81 cm² — halving as for a triangle; a parallelogram is two such triangles, so base × height in full.

me2-trapezium-area.shortcut: Split it into a 12 × 10 rectangle (120) and side triangles with a combined base of 8 (½ × 8 × 10 = 40): 160.
me2-trapezium-area.trap: 200 cm² — multiplying the longer parallel side by the height (20 × 10), as if it were a rectangle.

me2-wire-bent-into-square.shortcut: The side is a quarter of 2πr, i.e. πr/2 = (22/7 × 28) ÷ 2 = 44, and 44² = 1,936.
me2-wire-bent-into-square.trap: 3,136 cm² — taking the square's side as the circle's diameter (56 cm); the wire's 176 cm length gives a 44 cm side.

me2-square-area-increase.trap: 40% — doubling the 20% as though area grew in step with the side; the extra 4% is the corner piece 0.2 × 0.2.

me2-cube-volume-increase.shortcut: Picture a 2 × 2 × 2 stack: a cube with doubled edges is built from 8 of the original cubes.
me2-cube-volume-increase.trap: 4 — squaring the factor as for area; volume has three dimensions, so 2³.

me2-room-four-walls.shortcut: Two 8 × 4 walls (64) and two 6 × 4 walls (48) make 112 m².
me2-room-four-walls.trap: 128 m² — treating all four walls as 8 m × 4 m; two of them are only 6 m wide.

ls-squares-plus-one.shortcut: Parity alternates even, odd, even, odd, even, so the next term is odd (35 or 37); the gaps 3, 5, 7, 9 call for 11, not 9.
ls-squares-plus-one.trap: 35 — repeating the last gap of 9 instead of letting the odd gaps grow to 11.

ls-multiply-add-alternating.shortcut: The gaps 4, 8, 16, 32 double each time, so the next gap is 64: 63 + 64 = 127.
ls-multiply-add-alternating.trap: 95 — repeating the last gap of 32 instead of doubling it to 64.

ls-alternating-two-series.shortcut: The gaps alternate +6 and −3, and the sixth term follows a −3, so it takes +6: 11 + 6 = 17.
ls-alternating-two-series.trap: 18 — reading the upward jumps as growing (+6, then +7); they stay at +6, while each alternate series climbs by a steady 3.

ls-letter-skip-two.shortcut: Skip two letters each time: after J drop K and L, landing on M.
ls-letter-skip-two.trap: "L" — skipping only one letter after J; the series skips two each time (B, C after A; E, F after D).

ls-fibonacci-like.shortcut: Test the rule on the last three: 10 + 16 = 26 confirms add-the-previous-two, so 16 + 26 = 42.
ls-fibonacci-like.trap: 36 — repeating the last gap of 10; each gap equals the term two places back, so the next gap is 16.

ls-odd-one-out-series.shortcut: The run is 2³ to 6³ with 100 wedged between 4³ and 5³; a cube between 64 and 125 would need a whole number between 4 and 5, and none exists.
ls-odd-one-out-series.trap: 64 — it is also a square (8²), so a candidate hunting for the 'square' may pick it; but 64 = 4³ fits the cube run, while 100 is only a square.

cd-shift-by-one.shortcut: Check one letter per option: D must become E (drops DPH) and G must become H (drops EPG); FQI shifts by two, leaving EPH.
cd-shift-by-one.trap: "DPH" — keeping the D because the code DBU already starts with D; every letter moves one step, so D → E.

cd-reverse-and-shift.shortcut: The code's first letter is the word's last letter + 1: N → O leaves OFQ and OQF, and the middle E → F picks OFQ.
cd-reverse-and-shift.trap: "QFO" — shifting each letter but forgetting to reverse; BOOK's code LPPC reads CPPL backwards, so the reversal is part of the rule.

cd-number-code-sum.shortcut: Only the units digit matters: P, I, N, K are 16, 9, 14, 11, and 6 + 9 + 4 + 1 ends in 0, so 50 is the only possible option.
cd-number-code-sum.trap: 48 — misplacing N as the 12th letter instead of the 14th; the units digits already demand an answer ending in 0.

cd-substitution-language.shortcut: Pit, na, lat and tuk each appear once, so none can mean 'water', which occurs in both meanings; som is the only survivor.
cd-substitution-language.trap: "lat" — it sits beside som in the second sentence and a quick reader pairs it with 'water'; lat appears in one sentence only, so it must be 'is' or 'cold'.

cd-position-value-shift.shortcut: Test one letter per option: S + 3 = V drops CWU, B + 1 = C drops DWV, U + 2 = W drops CVV — leaving CWV.
cd-position-value-shift.trap: "CWU" — carrying the middle shift of +2 into the third letter; the shifts rise +1, +2, +3, so S → V.

br-only-son-of-father.shortcut: Replace 'the only son of my father' with 'me': the photograph shows 'the son of me', so the speaker is the father.
br-only-son-of-father.trap: "Brother" — reading 'son of my father' as a brother; the word 'only' rules a brother out, so the phrase points back to the speaker.

br-brother-of-mother.shortcut: She and the speaker are in the same generation (both grandchildren of the mother's parents) but not siblings, which makes her a cousin.
br-brother-of-mother.trap: "Niece" — she is the mother's niece, not the speaker's; a niece is a sibling's child, one generation below.

br-woman-photo-daughter.shortcut: Swap 'the only daughter of my mother' for 'me': the girl is 'my daughter'.
br-woman-photo-daughter.trap: "Niece" — reading 'daughter of my mother' as a sister and her child as a niece; 'only' means the speaker has no sister.

br-family-of-six.shortcut: Count generations: A and E sit two above C and D (A → B → C, D), so E, a woman, is the grandmother.
br-family-of-six.trap: "Mother" — E is B's mother; transferring that relation to D skips a generation.

ds-walk-and-turn.shortcut: Two right turns reverse the heading, so the third leg undoes the first; only the 15 m middle leg, heading east, remains.
ds-walk-and-turn.trap: "15 m west" — taking a right turn from north as west; facing north, right is east.

ds-shadow-direction.shortcut: Morning shadows point west; with west on his right hand, the man faces north (east on his left).
ds-shadow-direction.trap: "South" — putting the sun in the west, so the shadow points east; east on the right means facing south.

ds-pythagoras-displacement.shortcut: The distance must be under 6 + 8 = 14 and over 8; 6-8-10 is the 3-4-5 triangle doubled.
ds-pythagoras-displacement.trap: 14 km — adding the two legs, which is the distance walked, not the straight-line distance from the start.

ds-left-turns.shortcut: Net the turns: left + left + right is one left, and a left from south faces east.
ds-left-turns.trap: "West" — turning left from south as it looks on a map; facing south, the person's left hand points east.

sy-all-cats-animals.shortcut: Chain the 'all' statements forward: cats → animals → living things gives I; II runs the chain backwards, and 'all A are B' never turns into 'all B are A'.
sy-all-cats-animals.trap: "Both I and II" — reversing the 'all' statements; plenty of living things (trees, dogs) are not cats.

sy-some-pens-are-books.shortcut: One counter-drawing kills II: draw papers larger than books, so some paper is not a book. I survives every drawing because the pen-books sit inside papers.
sy-some-pens-are-books.trap: "Both I and II" — reading 'All books are papers' backwards as 'all papers are books'.

sy-no-a-is-b.shortcut: 'Some lazy are rich' plus 'no lazy is a student' gives the standard 'some rich are not students'; a 'no' conclusion needs both premises universal.
sy-no-a-is-b.trap: "Both" — stretching 'some rich people are not students' to 'no rich person is a student'; rich people who are not lazy may still be students.

sa-row-of-five.shortcut: With C and E fixed at the ends, the A–B pair and D fill seats 2–4; D comes after B, so the pair must start at seat 2, putting B in seat 3.
sa-row-of-five.trap: "A" — placing B to A's left by reading 'right' from the viewer's side, which gives C, B, A, D, E; facing north, B immediately right of A gives C, A, B, D, E.

sa-circle-of-six.shortcut: Six seats make three opposite pairs; P–S and Q–R are two of them, so T and U must be the third — no need to fix left and right.
sa-circle-of-six.trap: "P" — T sits right beside S and S is opposite P, so a hurried reader carries 'opposite P' over to T; T's opposite is the one person left unpaired, U.

an-doctor-hospital.shortcut: Hospital is a place of work; School is the only option that is a place.
an-doctor-hospital.trap: "Student" — it follows 'works with' (doctor : patient), a different relation from 'works in'.

an-odd-one-out-words.shortcut: Name the category of the first two — flowers — and test each item against it: only Mango is a fruit.
an-odd-one-out-words.trap: "Marigold" — it shares the 'Ma' opening with Mango and is less of a bouquet flower than rose or jasmine, but it is still a flower; Mango alone is a fruit.

an-square-cube-analogy.shortcut: Only one option ends in 4, the units digit of 12²: 144.
an-square-cube-analogy.trap: 132 — 12 × 11, a product of neighbours that looks square-like; 81 is 9 × 9, so the partner is 12 × 12.

mr-data-sufficiency-age.shortcut: Ask what each statement fixes: I gives only a gap and II only the brother's age; a gap plus one age fixes Ravi (19 + 5).
mr-data-sufficiency-age.trap: "II alone is enough" — it pins the brother at 19, and a hurried reader forgets the question asks for Ravi's age.

mr-clock-angle.shortcut: At 3:30 the hour hand is halfway between 3 and 4 and the minute hand is on 6: 2½ hour-gaps × 30° = 75°.
mr-clock-angle.trap: 90° — leaving the hour hand on the 3; in 30 minutes it moves 15° towards the 4.

mr-calendar-day.shortcut: Four weeks after Saturday 15 August is Saturday 12 September; three days more is Tuesday the 15th.
mr-calendar-day.trap: "Monday" — counting August as 30 days (2 odd days); August has 31, which is 3 odd days.

mr-statement-and-assumption.shortcut: Negate each: if nobody wanted a first-attempt pass the advert would fall flat, so I is needed; if other routes exist the advert still stands, so II is not.
mr-statement-and-assumption.trap: "Both" — accepting II because the advert sounds exclusive; it promises success, not that it is the only way.
